entities.name: Arnaud de Pellegrue
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Arnaud de Pellegrue (died 1331) was a pivotal cardinal-nephew to Pope Clement V, the architect of the Avignon Papacy, playing a crucial role in the nascent stages of this seventy-year period of papal residence outside Rome. His elevation in 1305, shortly after his uncle's election, exemplifies the pervasive nepotism that characterized medieval papal courts, yet his influence extended beyond mere familial ties. Pellegrue was instrumental in consolidating the administrative and diplomatic machinery of the papacy during its relocation, helping to establish Avignon as the new center of Catholic ecclesiastical power.

Elevated to cardinal-priest of Santa Cecilia in 1305 and subsequently cardinal-bishop of Albano, Pellegrue served as a trusted advisor and executor of papal policy. He undertook a significant legation to Italy from 1306 to 1307, attempting to reassert papal temporal authority in regions like Tuscany and Romagna amidst rampant Guelph-Ghibelline conflicts, though with limited lasting success. Furthermore, he participated in the drawn-out papal election of 1314–1316, which eventually saw John XXII ascend to the pontificate, further solidifying the Avignon presence. His administrative acumen was vital in managing the Holy See's finances and diplomatic relations during a period of profound institutional transition.

Pellegrue's career helped shape the institutional framework of the Avignon Papacy, contributing to its centralized bureaucracy and financial mechanisms that would persist for decades. His active participation in the suppression of the Knights Templar, following Clement V's directives, underscores his involvement in one of the most controversial decisions of the era, which saw the Order dissolved and its assets seized. The consolidation of papal power in Avignon, facilitated by figures like Pellegrue, enabled the papacy to operate with greater independence from Roman aristocratic factions, albeit under the increasing influence of the French monarchy.

His career exemplifies the profound institutional changes within the Catholic Church during the early 14th century.
